title: Final Accounts of Non-Manufacturing Entities
outcomes: Explain what final accounts are and how the income statement (Trading and Profit and Loss Account) and the position statement (Balance Sheet) fit together.
Apply the basic rules for preparing final accounts — capital vs revenue, business vs personal, period cut-off and the matching principle.
Prepare a Trading Account, a Profit and Loss Account and a Balance Sheet of a sole trader from a trial balance with year-end adjustments.
Handle the common adjustments: outstanding, prepaid, accrued and advance items; bad debts and provisions; depreciation; fire loss; goods taken, given away or on approval; manager's commission.
Pass closing entries and the opening entry, distinguish provisions from reserves, and explain the limitations of financial statements.

meta.exam_tip: A final-accounts question is a marks bank: every adjustment carries step marks in two places. Tick each adjustment twice (P&L side and Balance Sheet side) as you use it, and show workings for debtors, depreciation and capital.

concepts.title: Final accounts of a trading business
body: A non-manufacturing (trading) entity buys goods and sells them in the same form — it does not process them. At the year end it prepares financial statements to learn two things: how much it earned (performance) and what it owns and owes (position).

The income statement is in two stages — the Trading Account (gross profit or gross loss) and the Profit and Loss Account (net profit or net loss). The position statement is the Balance Sheet. Together they are traditionally called "final accounts", though the Balance Sheet is a statement, not an account.

The income statement covers a period ("for the year ended"); the Balance Sheet speaks of one moment ("as at"). Larger entities may add a cash flow statement and other statements; these are not compulsory for a sole trader.
concepts.analogy: The income statement is a video of the year's business; the Balance Sheet is a photograph taken at the closing moment.
concepts.work: Banks ask small traders for final accounts before sanctioning a working-capital limit, and income-tax returns of proprietors are built on these figures. Preparing them is bread-and-butter work for a CA in practice.

concepts.title: Ground rules and the matching principle
body: Before drafting final accounts: (a) keep the proprietor's personal income and expenses out of the business figures; (b) separate capital from revenue, for both receipts and payments; (c) disclose every material item (an unusual bonus to staff, a big inventory write-off); (d) cut off the year's transactions from the next year's; (e) record only transactions completed by the year end — goods awaiting the buyer's inspection are not yet sales.

The two statements are linked: of the money spent, part is charged to P&L and the unused part sits in the Balance Sheet (machinery less depreciation; salaries paid plus outstanding salaries as a liability).

Matching principle: charge against revenue all the expenses incurred to earn it, paid or not (hence outstanding expenses and opening stock in the Trading Account); carry forward costs that will earn next year's revenue (prepaid expenses, unexpired cost of assets); and treat money received for next year's work as income received in advance (a liability).
Exception: losses that earn no revenue — uninsured fire loss, stock falling below cost, debts turning bad — are still charged at once, or profit would be overstated.
concepts.analogy: Like a cricket scorecard for one match: runs scored and balls bowled in this match only — not the next match's practice sessions.
concepts.work: Cut-off testing is a standard audit procedure: the auditor checks invoices dated just before and after 31 March to make sure sales and purchases are booked in the right year.

concepts.title: The Trading Account
body: Debit side: opening stock; purchases less purchase returns; direct expenses — every cost of bringing goods to their present location and condition (carriage/freight inwards, godown wages, customs duty, dock charges, octroi, royalty on goods). Credit side: sales less sales returns; closing stock. Balancing figure: gross profit (debit side, carried to P&L credit) or gross loss.
Freight or wages spent on installing a fixed asset is added to that asset's cost, not charged to Trading. Goods received at year end without an invoice are still recorded as purchases.

Closing stock is taken at the lower of its cost and its net realisable value, and includes goods with agents on consignment and goods sent on approval. If stock is counted a few days before or after the year end, adjust it to the closing date (sales after the year end are added back at cost, purchases after the year end are deducted).

If closing stock already appears in the trial balance (adjusted through purchases), it goes only to the Balance Sheet. Closing entries: Trading A/c Dr, To Opening Stock, To Purchases, To direct expenses; Sales A/c Dr and Closing Stock A/c Dr, To Trading A/c; then Trading A/c Dr, To P&L A/c (gross profit).
concepts.analogy: The Trading Account is a shopkeeper's counter view — what did the goods cost me to get on the shelf, and what did I sell them for?
concepts.work: Gross profit ratio is the first number an analyst or lender looks at. A sudden fall usually means stock was undervalued, purchases were booked in the wrong year, or there was theft — all things a CA probes.

concepts.title: The Profit and Loss Account
body: Starts with gross profit (credit) or gross loss (debit). Debit: all indirect expenses and losses of the year, grouped by function — administration (office salaries, rent, audit fees, legal charges, printing and stationery, electricity), selling and distribution (advertisement, carriage outwards, selling commission, bad debts and provision), finance (interest on loans, bank charges, discount allowed) and abnormal losses (loss by fire, loss on sale of assets). Credit: other incomes — discount received, commission, interest, rent from property let out, dividends, profit on sale of assets.
Balancing figure: net profit (debit side), transferred to Capital A/c — P&L A/c Dr, To Capital A/c; net loss — Capital A/c Dr, To P&L A/c.

Not charged to P&L: drawings (they reduce capital); the proprietor's income tax (his personal liability, so it is drawings); trade discount (already netted in the invoice). Rebate given to customers who cross a sales target is debited to Rebate A/c and closed to P&L. Bad debts recovered are a gain, credited to P&L, not to the customer.
concepts.analogy: If the Trading Account is the counter, the P&L is the whole shop: rent, staff, electricity and interest all come out of the counter's gross profit before the owner sees his net profit.
concepts.work: Disallowances in tax audits often start here — personal expenses of the proprietor booked as business expenses. A CA must reclassify them as drawings before signing.

concepts.title: Adjustments for outstanding, prepaid, accrued and advance items
body: Outstanding (accrued) expense: Expense A/c Dr, To Outstanding Expense A/c — added to the expense, shown as a liability.
Prepaid expense: Prepaid Expense A/c Dr, To Expense A/c — deducted from the expense, shown as an asset.
Accrued income: Accrued Income A/c Dr, To Income A/c — added to the income, shown as an asset.
Income received in advance: Income A/c Dr, To Income Received in Advance A/c — deducted from the income, shown as a liability.

Stock of stationery or similar materials unused at year end is deducted from that expense and shown as an asset. "Outstanding" is used when payment is already due; "accrued" when it relates to the year but falls due later. All these entries are reversed at the start of the next year.

blocks.title: Every adjustment hits two places

concepts.analogy: You pay a year's gym membership in February: by 31 March only two months are "used". The remaining ten months are still yours — a prepaid asset.
concepts.work: Year-end "provisions for expenses" (audit fee, electricity bill not yet received, interest due) are a standard closing checklist item in every accounts department.

concepts.title: Bad debts, provision for doubtful debts and provision for discount
body: Bad debt: an amount certainly irrecoverable — Bad Debts A/c Dr, To Debtor; closed to P&L (or set against an existing provision).
Provision for doubtful debts: a prudent estimate of debts that may not be collected — P&L A/c Dr, To Provision for Doubtful Debts. Customers' accounts are not touched until a debt actually goes bad.

Order of working in exams: (1) write off further bad debts from debtors; (2) compute the new provision on the remaining debtors; (3) P&L charge = bad debts (old + further) + new provision − old provision (a negative result is a credit to P&L); (4) Balance Sheet: debtors less further bad debts less new provision.
Provision for discount on debtors is calculated on debtors after deducting further bad debts and the doubtful-debts provision.
concepts.analogy: An umbrella: you buy it (create the provision) before it rains; when rain (an actual bad debt) comes, it falls on the umbrella first, not on your clothes (this year's profit).
concepts.work: Ageing analysis of receivables — how long each invoice has been unpaid — is the usual basis for the provision. Auditors challenge a provision that has not moved while overdue balances have grown.

concepts.title: Other common adjustments
body: Depreciation: P&L debit; deducted from the asset in the Balance Sheet. Interest on capital: P&L debit, added to capital. Interest on drawings: P&L credit, deducted from capital.

Abnormal loss of stock by fire or accident: Loss by Fire A/c Dr, To Purchases (or Trading A/c) with the full cost; then Insurance Claim A/c Dr (admitted amount) and P&L A/c Dr (balance), To Loss by Fire A/c. The claim is an asset until received.

Goods used other than for sale are removed from purchases at cost and debited to the right head: Drawings (personal use), Advertisement (free samples), Charity/Donation, the asset account (used to build an asset) or Repairs (used in maintenance).
Goods on approval at year end, still unaccepted: Sales A/c Dr, To Debtor (selling price); and Stock on Approval A/c Dr, To Trading A/c (cost), so they enter closing stock.

Manager's commission on net profit: before charging it = profit before commission × rate/100; after charging it = profit before commission × rate/(100 + rate). Commission A/c Dr, To Commission Payable A/c — P&L debit and a liability.
concepts.analogy: Commission "after charging" is like a 10% service charge that is itself part of the bill — you cannot just take 10% of the total; you must take 10/110 of it.
concepts.work: Profit-linked incentives are common in family businesses. The CA must compute them on the agreed basis; using the wrong formula overpays the manager and understates profit.

concepts.title: The Balance Sheet
body: A statement of assets, liabilities and capital as at a particular date — true only for that moment, which is why it says "as at". It is prepared after the P&L, because closing capital needs the net profit. Since capital = assets − liabilities, the two sides must agree; if not, there is an error.

Order of presentation: by liquidity (cash first, land and building last; current liabilities first, capital last) or by permanence (fixed assets first, cash last; capital first). Investments may be placed by the owner's intention.

Classification: current assets (expected to turn into cash within about a year — stock, debtors, bank, cash, prepaid expenses); non-current or fixed assets (machinery, building, long-term investments); intangible assets (patents, copyrights, goodwill). Liabilities: current (payable within a year — creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses) and long-term (term loans).
Sole traders usually use the horizontal form: capital and liabilities on the left, assets on the right. Capital is shown as opening balance + net profit (− net loss) − drawings.
concepts.analogy: A Balance Sheet is a selfie of the business at the stroke of midnight on 31 March — one second later, something has changed.
concepts.work: Lenders compute ratios like current ratio and debt–equity straight off the Balance Sheet. Misclassifying a long-term loan as current can push a client into a loan-covenant breach.

concepts.title: The accounting cycle and the opening entry
body: Sequence: record transactions in the journal (and subsidiary books) → post to the ledger → prepare the trial balance → prepare the Trading and Profit and Loss Account → prepare the Balance Sheet. Next year the cycle restarts.

Opening entry: the first journal entry of a new year, bringing the previous Balance Sheet's balances into the new books — all asset accounts debited; all liability accounts, provisions and capital credited. Nominal accounts never appear in it because they were closed to Trading/P&L.
concepts.analogy: Closing a school year and opening a new notebook: the first page lists what you are carrying over from last year.
concepts.work: When a CA takes over books from a previous accountant, the first check is that the opening balances in the software agree with last year's audited Balance Sheet.

concepts.title: Provisions and reserves
body: Provision: an amount charged to cover depreciation, renewal or a fall in asset values, or a liability that is known to exist but cannot be measured precisely — e.g. provision for doubtful debts, for tax not yet assessed, for discounts. It is a charge against profit and must be made whether there is profit or loss.

Reserve: an appropriation of profit (revenue or capital) set aside for a general or specific purpose, other than covering a known liability or a fall in asset values. Types: revenue reserves (from trading profits) and capital reserves (from capital profits). Any excess provision beyond what is needed is in substance a reserve.
Reserve fund: a reserve whose amount is invested outside the business in readily saleable securities, for example to replace an asset in future.
concepts.analogy: A provision is money you keep aside because a bill is surely coming; a reserve is savings you choose to keep for a rainy day.
concepts.work: Under-providing for doubtful debts or tax inflates profit; over-providing creates "secret reserves". Both distort the accounts — auditors test provisions for adequacy and for excess.

concepts.title: Limitations of financial statements
body: Historical cost: items are recorded at the money value when the transaction happened; later price changes are ignored, so an old building may appear at a fraction of its present worth.
Intangible strengths and weaknesses — such as the skill and loyalty of staff — do not appear at all.

Going concern versus yearly accounts: the business is assumed to last indefinitely, yet results are cut into years, so many costs (depreciation, deferred items) are spread on estimates — the figures are not exact.

Different accounting policies (valuation methods, treatment of retirement benefits or intangibles) are allowed within limits, so comparing two businesses can mislead unless both follow the same basis. Management's own policies also shape the figures.
concepts.analogy: A Balance Sheet is like a family photo from years ago kept in today's album — accurate for when it was taken, but not a picture of today.
concepts.work: When advising on a business purchase or a loan, a CA adjusts reported figures (revaluing property, aligning accounting policies) before drawing conclusions.

illustrations.title: Complete final accounts with ten adjustments
illustrations.q: From the trial balance of Rao Stores and the information below, prepare for the year ended 31 March 2027 the Trading Account, the Profit and Loss Account and, as at that date, the Balance Sheet. (1) Closing stock at cost ₹1,45,000 (its net realisable value is higher). (2) Salaries outstanding ₹12,000. (3) Rent includes ₹6,000 for April 2027. (4) Insurance prepaid ₹3,000. (5) Write off further bad debts ₹5,000 and keep the provision for doubtful debts at 5% of debtors. (6) Depreciate furniture at 10% and the motor van at 20%. (7) Interest on the bank loan is unpaid. (8) Commission earned but not received ₹2,000. (9) Goods costing ₹4,000 taken by the proprietor were not recorded. (10) Goods costing ₹6,000 were destroyed by fire; the insurer admitted a claim of ₹4,500 (not yet recorded).

illustrations.title: Manager's commission — before and after charging
illustrations.q: Net profit of Gupta Electronics before charging the manager's commission is ₹2,20,000. Compute the commission at 10% if it is payable (a) on net profit before charging such commission, (b) on net profit after charging such commission. Give the journal entry for case (b).

entries.narr: Being 10% commission on net profit after charging such commission, profit before commission ₹2,20,000

solution.title: Proof for (b)
solution.text: Profit after commission = 2,20,000 − 20,000 = ₹2,00,000, and 10% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹20,000 — the commission. Commission Payable is a current liability in the Balance Sheet.

In March, goods were sent to a customer on approval for ₹48,000 (cost plus 20%) and recorded as a sale; by 31 March the customer had approved goods worth ₹12,000 and the rest were with him, not counted in the stock. jobs.title: Closing the books of a retail client
jobs.role: Audit assistant at a CA firm preparing accounts for a proprietor
jobs.situation: A garment retailer hands you his trial balance on 15 April with a note: "rent of April paid in March, electricity bill for March not received, I took some shirts for my family, and one customer has shut shop owing ₹18,000." He wants final accounts by the month end for his bank.
steps: List each item as an adjustment with its two effects: prepaid rent (P&L less, asset), electricity outstanding (P&L more, liability), goods taken (purchases less, drawings more), bad debt (P&L, debtors less).
Get the stock sheet signed by the proprietor; value at lower of cost and net realisable value — old-season stock may need a write-down.
Review debtors for further doubtful amounts and agree the provision rate with him.
Prepare Trading, P&L and Balance Sheet; check that capital closes as opening + profit − drawings.
Explain to the proprietor why personal items reduce capital rather than appear as expenses.
jobs.takeaway: Every adjustment is a pair of entries; missing either half breaks the Balance Sheet.
jobs.think: The proprietor says, "Show the shirts as advertisement — it saves tax." What should you do?
jobs.answer: Refuse. Goods for personal use are drawings; recording them as a business expense misstates profit and is improper. Explain the treatment and record them correctly.

jobs.title: Reading final accounts for a loan proposal
jobs.situation: A trader's balance sheet shows land bought in 2009 at ₹6 lakh, rising profits and very low provisions for doubtful debts although debtors have doubled.
steps: Remember the historical-cost limitation: the land may be worth far more today, so get a valuation if it is offered as security.
Compare the provision with an ageing of debtors; a stale provision may be inflating profit.
Check whether stock is valued at cost or NRV and whether any slow-moving stock is included.
Ask about intangible factors the statements cannot show — key customers, staff, licences.
jobs.takeaway: Final accounts are the starting point of analysis, not the end — know their limitations.
jobs.think: Why might two traders with identical sales and costs report different profits?
jobs.answer: They may use different accounting policies — e.g. different depreciation methods or provisioning rates — which change reported profit without any change in actual business.

mcqs.q: Opening stock ₹50,000; purchases ₹3,00,000; carriage inwards ₹10,000; sales ₹4,50,000; closing stock ₹70,000. Gross profit is:
mcqs.explain: Cost of goods sold = opening stock 50,000 + purchases 3,00,000 + carriage inwards 10,000 − closing stock 70,000 = ₹2,90,000. Gross profit = sales 4,50,000 − 2,90,000 = ₹1,60,000. The trap is leaving out carriage inwards (giving ₹1,70,000): freight paid to bring goods into the godown is a direct cost. In practice: a kirana wholesaler's accountant loads inward freight into cost of goods, so the gross margin reflects the true landed cost.

mcqs.q: When closing stock appears in the trial balance, it is shown:
options: Only in the Balance Sheet
Only on the credit side of the Trading Account
In the Trading Account and the Balance Sheet
On the debit side of the Trading Account
mcqs.explain: If closing stock appears inside the trial balance, it has already been adjusted against purchases (an adjusted purchases figure). Crediting it to the Trading Account again would count it twice, so it goes only to the Balance Sheet as a current asset. The trap is the usual rule — Trading credit plus Balance Sheet — which applies only when closing stock is given outside the trial balance. In practice: ERP systems that post stock adjustments before closing produce exactly this kind of trial balance.

mcqs.q: Net profit before the manager's commission is ₹3,30,000. Commission at 10% on net profit after charging such commission is:
mcqs.explain: Commission 'after charging such commission' means commission = 10% of (profit − commission). So commission is 10/110 of the profit before commission: 3,30,000 × 10/110 = ₹30,000; check: 10% of 3,00,000 = 30,000. The trap ₹33,000 is 10% of the profit before commission. In practice: managers' incentive clauses in employment letters specify 'before' or 'after' commission, and the accountant must read that wording before computing the payout.

mcqs.q: Debtors ₹2,00,000; bad debts in the trial balance ₹4,000; further bad debts ₹10,000; provision to be 5% of debtors; old provision ₹6,000. The P&L charge for bad and doubtful debts is:
mcqs.explain: Total bad debts = 4,000 + 10,000 = ₹14,000. The new provision is on debtors after writing off the further bad debts: 5% of (2,00,000 − 10,000) = ₹9,500. P&L charge = 14,000 + 9,500 − old provision 6,000 = ₹17,500. The trap ₹18,000 takes 5% of ₹2,00,000, forgetting that the further bad debts must be removed first. In practice: a CA reviewing a distributor's books ensures provisions are computed only on debts still considered recoverable.

mcqs.q: The income tax of a sole proprietor paid out of the business bank account is:
options: Treated as drawings and deducted from capital
Debited to the Profit and Loss Account
Debited to the Trading Account
Shown as an asset
mcqs.explain: A sole proprietor's income tax is levied on his total income from all sources, so it is his personal liability, not a business expense. When paid from the business account it is treated as drawings and deducted from capital. Debiting it to Profit and Loss is the trap — that would understate business profit. In practice: when a proprietor pays advance tax from the shop's current account, the accountant books it to his drawings, never to expenses.

options: Profit and Loss Account (debit)
Trading Account (debit)
Balance Sheet (asset)
Trading Account (credit)
mcqs.explain: Carriage outwards is the cost of delivering goods to customers, so it is a selling and distribution expense and is debited to the Profit and Loss Account. The trap is the Trading Account, which takes carriage inwards — the cost of bringing goods to the place of business. In practice: e-commerce sellers track outward courier charges as a selling expense, which helps them judge whether free delivery is eating into net profit.

options: A provision is a charge against profit; a reserve is an appropriation of profit
A reserve is a charge against profit; a provision is an appropriation of profit
Both are appropriations of profit
A provision is created only when there is profit
mcqs.explain: A provision covers a known liability or a fall in an asset's value, so it is a charge against profit and must be made even in a loss year. A reserve is profit set aside voluntarily or by law, so it is an appropriation of profit. The trap is reversing the two, or thinking provisions need profits. In practice: a company must provide for doubtful debts and depreciation even in a loss year, but can create a general reserve only out of profits.

mcqs.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 were destroyed by fire and the insurer admitted ₹35,000. The amount debited to the P&L Account is:
mcqs.explain: Goods of ₹50,000 were lost but the insurer admitted ₹35,000, which becomes a claim receivable (an asset). Only the uninsured part, 50,000 − 35,000 = ₹15,000, is a real loss and is debited to Profit and Loss. The trap is debiting the full ₹50,000, which ignores the claim. In practice: after a godown fire, the accountant records the insurance claim as receivable on the surveyor's assessment and writes off only the shortfall.

mcqs.q: In a Balance Sheet arranged in order of liquidity, the first asset is:
options: Cash in hand
Land and building
Stock
Trade receivables
mcqs.explain: In the order of liquidity, assets are listed from the one most easily converted into cash to the least. Cash in hand is already cash, so it comes first, followed by bank, receivables, stock and finally fixed assets such as land. The trap is land and building, which comes first only in the order of permanence. In practice: banks and some sole traders present balance sheets in liquidity order, while companies follow Schedule III, which lists non-current items first.

mcqs.q: Goods sent on approval for ₹50,000 (cost plus 25%) are unapproved at the year end. They are added to closing stock at:
mcqs.explain: Goods sent on approval and not yet approved still belong to the seller, so they are part of closing stock at cost. Selling price ₹50,000 is cost plus 25%, so cost = 50,000 × 100/125 = ₹40,000. The trap ₹37,500 deducts 25% of the selling price, but the markup is 25% on cost. In practice: jewellers and furniture dealers who send goods on approval keep a register, and at year-end the unapproved items are added back to stock at cost.

mcqs.q: Wages paid for installing a new machine should be:
options: Added to the cost of the machine
Debited to the Trading Account
Debited to the P&L Account
Deducted from capital
mcqs.explain: Wages paid to install a new machine are a cost of getting a fixed asset ready for use, so they are capital expenditure and added to the cost of the machine (and depreciated over its life). The trap is debiting them to the Trading Account, where ordinary production wages go. In practice: when a factory installs new equipment, the accountant capitalises installation labour as part of the asset under AS 10.

mcqs.q: Stock at cost is ₹80,000 and its net realisable value is ₹72,000. Closing stock is shown at:
mcqs.explain: Inventory is carried at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower. Cost ₹80,000 is higher than NRV ₹72,000, so closing stock is shown at ₹72,000; the ₹8,000 fall is a loss recognised now. The trap is ₹80,000 — showing stock at cost even though it will fetch less, which breaks prudence. In practice: garment retailers write down last season's stock to NRV at year-end because it will sell only at a discount.

mcqs.q: The correct sequence of the accounting cycle is:
options: Journal → Ledger → Trial balance → Trading and P&L → Balance Sheet
Ledger → Journal → Trial balance → Balance Sheet → P&L
Journal → Trial balance → Ledger → P&L → Balance Sheet
Trial balance → Journal → Ledger → Balance Sheet → P&L
mcqs.explain: Transactions are first recorded in the journal, then posted to ledger accounts, balances are tested in the trial balance, and from it the Trading and Profit and Loss Account is prepared before the Balance Sheet (which needs the net profit for capital). The trap is putting the trial balance before the ledger — you cannot list balances you have not yet posted. In practice: accounting software follows the same cycle: vouchers, ledgers, trial balance, then financial statements.
mcqs.topic: Sequence of Accounting Procedure or the Accounting Cycle

options: Assets are debited; liabilities and capital are credited
Assets are credited; liabilities and capital are debited
Expenses are debited; incomes are credited
Only cash and capital are recorded
mcqs.explain: The opening entry brings forward last year's closing balances. Assets have debit balances, so they are debited; liabilities and capital have credit balances, so they are credited. The trap is the reverse, or debiting expenses — nominal accounts are closed at year-end and do not carry forward. In practice: when a business switches to new accounting software, its opening balances are entered through exactly such an opening entry.

mcqs.q: Rent received includes ₹8,000 for the next year. The ₹8,000 is shown as:
options: A liability (income received in advance)
An asset (accrued income)
An addition to rent received in P&L
An expense in P&L
mcqs.explain: Rent of ₹8,000 for the next year has been received but not yet earned. It is deducted from rent received in Profit and Loss and shown as a liability — income received in advance — because the business owes the tenant use of the property. The trap is 'accrued income', which is income earned but not yet received (an asset). In practice: landlords and coaching institutes collecting fees in advance show the unearned part as a liability at year-end.

questions.q: Explain any four limitations of financial statements.

items: Historical cost: assets are carried at what they cost when bought, so price changes since then are ignored and old assets look understated.
Intangible strengths and weaknesses — staff skill, customer loyalty, management quality — are not shown at all.
Periodic accounts of a continuing business: costs such as depreciation are spread over years on estimates, so annual figures are approximations.

Different accounting policies (stock valuation, depreciation methods, treatment of retirement benefits) are permitted, so comparison between businesses can mislead; management policies also influence the figures.

remarks: Each point should be explained in one or two lines; one-word lists earn little.
mistakes: Listing errors of book-keeping (which a trial balance may catch) as limitations of statements.
tips: Number your points and give a short example for each.

summary: Trading A/c → gross profit (opening stock, net purchases, direct expenses vs net sales, closing stock). P&L → net profit (indirect expenses vs other incomes). Balance Sheet → position as at the year end.
Matching: charge all expenses of the year (paid or not), carry forward costs for next year, defer income received in advance; losses are charged immediately.
Each adjustment has two effects — one in Trading/P&L and one in the Balance Sheet.
Bad debts → new provision on remaining debtors → charge = bad debts + new − old provision; discount provision comes after.
Commission on profit: before = P × r/100; after = P × r/(100 + r).
Provision = charge against profit; reserve = appropriation of profit. Opening entry: assets Dr, liabilities and capital Cr.
remember: Closing stock in the trial balance → Balance Sheet only.
Drawings and proprietor's income tax never go to P&L.
Stock is taken at cost or net realisable value, whichever is less.
traps: Don't value goods on approval at selling price — use cost.
Don't calculate the new provision before deducting further bad debts.
Don't forget to add goods taken by the proprietor to drawings when reducing purchases.

viva.q: What is the difference between the Trading Account and the Profit and Loss Account?
viva.model: The Trading Account works out gross profit. It contains opening stock, net purchases, direct expenses such as carriage inwards and godown wages, net sales and closing stock. The Profit and Loss Account works out net profit, starting from the gross profit. It is debited with indirect expenses such as office, selling and finance expenses and losses, and credited with other incomes. The net profit is transferred to the capital account.

viva.q: Explain the matching principle and how it affects the year-end adjustments.
viva.model: The matching principle says that the expenses incurred to earn the revenue of a period must be charged in the same period. So outstanding expenses of the year are added even if not paid, prepaid expenses relating to next year are carried forward as an asset, and income received in advance is shown as a liability and not as this year's income.

viva.q: How is closing stock valued and where is it shown in the final accounts?
viva.model: Closing stock is taken at cost or net realisable value, whichever is less. If it is given outside the trial balance, it is credited to the Trading Account and also shown as a current asset in the Balance Sheet. If it already appears in the trial balance, it has been adjusted against purchases, so it is shown only in the Balance Sheet.

viva.q: Distinguish between a provision and a reserve.
viva.model: A provision is a charge against profit made for a known liability or a fall in the value of an asset whose amount cannot be fixed exactly, like a provision for doubtful debts or depreciation. A reserve is an appropriation of profit, set aside to strengthen the business or for a future purpose, and not for any known liability. A provision must be made even if there is a loss, but a reserve is created only out of profits.

viva.q: How do you calculate a manager's commission on net profit before and after charging such commission?
viva.model: If the commission is on net profit before charging it, commission equals the profit before commission multiplied by the rate over 100. If the commission is on net profit after charging it, commission equals the profit before commission multiplied by the rate over 100 plus the rate. For example, at 10 percent after charging, it is profit into 10 by 110.

viva.q: State the main limitations of financial statements.
viva.model: Financial statements are based on historical cost, so they ignore later changes in the value of money and prices. They do not show intangible strengths and weaknesses such as the skill and loyalty of staff. Because the business is assumed to continue but accounts are prepared every year, many costs are spread over years on an estimated basis, so the figures are not exact. And different businesses may follow different accounting policies, which makes comparison difficult.

cases.title: Year-end at Saanvi Fashions
cases.case: Saanvi Fashions' trial balance at 31 March 2027 shows: opening stock ₹90,000; purchases ₹5,80,000; carriage inwards ₹20,000; sales ₹9,00,000; salaries ₹1,26,000; rent ₹30,000; bad debts ₹3,000; provision for doubtful debts (credit) ₹2,500; interest received ₹5,000; trade receivables ₹1,50,000; depreciation for the year ₹18,000 (already worked out). Closing stock is ₹1,10,000. Additional information: further bad debts ₹3,000 are to be written off and the provision is to be kept at 4% of debtors.

mcqs.explain: Trading Account credit side: sales 9,00,000 + closing stock 1,10,000 = ₹10,10,000. Debit side: opening stock 90,000 + purchases 5,80,000 + carriage inwards 20,000 = ₹6,90,000. Gross profit = 10,10,000 − 6,90,000 = ₹3,20,000. The trap is charging salaries and rent in the Trading Account; they are indirect expenses for Profit and Loss. In practice: a fashion retailer tracks gross margin to price its collections, so only direct costs belong above the gross-profit line.

mcqs.q: What is the net amount charged to P&L for bad and doubtful debts?
mcqs.explain: Bad debts = 3,000 in the trial balance + 3,000 further = ₹6,000. New provision = 4% of debtors after write-off: 4% × (1,50,000 − 3,000) = ₹5,880. Charge to P&L = 6,000 + 5,880 − old provision 2,500 = ₹9,380. The trap ₹8,880 counts the bad debts only once. In practice: the accountant of a retail chain reviews debtor ageing at year-end, writes off hopeless dues, and tops up the provision to the agreed percentage.

Net profit = gross profit 3,20,000 + interest received 5,000 − salaries 1,26,000 − rent 30,000 − bad and doubtful debts 9,380 − depreciation 18,000 = ₹1,41,620. The usual trap is forgetting the interest income or using only the trial-balance bad debts instead of the full adjusted charge. In practice: the proprietor's income-tax return is built on this net profit, so each adjustment directly changes the tax payable.

mcqs.q: At what amount do trade receivables appear in the balance sheet?
mcqs.explain: Trade receivables are shown net: 1,50,000 − further bad debts 3,000 − new provision 5,880 = ₹1,41,120. The trap ₹1,47,000 removes the bad debts but forgets to deduct the provision for doubtful debts; ₹1,50,000 ignores both. In practice: lenders assessing drawing power on a cash-credit account look at net receivables after provisions, not the gross ledger total.
